title: Functorial additive Jordan decomposition of algebraic Lie elements and faithful detection
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], with a fixed algebraic closure $\bar k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $H$ be an affine $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Write $\mathfrak h=T_{H/k,e}$ for its tangent space at the identity [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space], with its bracket [def-wf-lie-algebra]. A finite-dimensional rational representation means a homomorphism of $k$-group schemes $r:H\to\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$ for an integer $n\geq1$ [def-sc-general-linear-group], and $dr:\mathfrak h\to\operatorname{Mat}_n(k)$ is its differential. A matrix is geometrically semisimple if it becomes diagonalizable over $\bar k$, and is nilpotent if some positive power is zero. If $k$ is perfect (every algebraic extension of $k$ is separable), then each $Y\in\mathfrak h$ has a unique decomposition $Y=Y_s+Y_n$, with $[Y_s,Y_n]=0$, such that for every finite-dimensional rational representation $r$, $dr(Y_s)$ and $dr(Y_n)$ are respectively the geometrically semisimple and nilpotent commuting parts of the additive Jordan decomposition of $dr(Y)$. This decomposition is preserved by differentials of homomorphisms between affine finite-type $k$-group schemes and by extension between perfect fields. For arbitrary $k$, if $i:H\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_{m,k}$ is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion], then $di$ is injective, and for every $Y\in\mathfrak h$ and every finite-dimensional rational representation $r$, geometric semisimplicity of $di(Y)$ implies geometric semisimplicity of $dr(Y)$, and nilpotence of $di(Y)$ implies nilpotence of $dr(Y)$. These statements concern differentials of algebraic group representations; they impose no assertion about arbitrary representations of the abstract Lie algebra.

source.place: Proposition 17.74(a),(b), printed p.377, and the geometric faithful-matrix formulation obtained by applying it over an algebraic closure. Rational representations, not arbitrary abstract Lie representations; Sections 10a–10d give tangent injectivity and matrix differentials. The theorem is the additive counterpart of Chapter 9 and does not assert a Jordan decomposition over an imperfect base field.

proof.text: Choose a closed faithful representation $i:H\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_{m,k}$ by [lem-sfb-affine-group-faithful-linear-representation]. Use the tangent Lie structure and matrix formula of [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus]. The map $di$ is injective over every field: if $di(X)=di(X')$, the dual-number formula gives $i(t_X)=i(t_{X'})$; faithfulness on the algebra $k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ gives $t_X=t_{X'}$, hence $X=X'$. The same argument applies after scalar extension, since the faithful-representation node gives injectivity on all algebra-valued points. No smoothness is involved.

Assume $k$ perfect. For every finite-dimensional rational representation $V$ (including zero), write $A_V=dr_V(Y)$ and take its linear parts $S_V,N_V$ using [lem-sfb-additive-jordan-linear-compatibility]. If $f:V\to W$ is equivariant, evaluate equivariance at $t_Y$ and compare coefficients of $\epsilon$ in $f(1+\epsilon A_V)=(1+\epsilon A_W)f$; thus $fA_V=A_Wf$ and $fS_V=S_Wf$, $fN_V=N_Wf$. For a tensor representation, $(1+\epsilon A_V)\otimes(1+\epsilon A_W)=1+\epsilon(A_V\otimes1+1\otimes A_W)$ because $\epsilon^2=0$. The tensor-sum clause gives $S_{V\otimes W}=S_V\otimes1+1\otimes S_W$, and the identical formula for $N$. On the trivial representation $A=0$, whose unique parts are both zero. These computations use the dual-number differential formula of [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus].

source.place: Proposition 17.74 exercise, p.377: additive analogues of 9.13--9.15; dual-number formula 10.7.

proof.text: Set $R=k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. For each of the two families put $\lambda^s_V=1+\epsilon S_V$ and $\lambda^n_V=1+\epsilon N_V$ on $V_R$. Their inverses are $1-\epsilon S_V$ and $1-\epsilon N_V$. The previous intertwiner, tensor-sum and unit identities give exactly all hypotheses of [lem-sfb-affine-group-tensor-reconstruction], since $(1+\epsilon S_V)\otimes_R(1+\epsilon S_W)=1+\epsilon(S_V\otimes1+1\otimes S_W)$. Reconstruct $t_s,t_n\in H(R)$. Their reductions in $H(k)$ have identity image under $i$, so are the identity by faithfulness [lem-sfb-affine-group-faithful-linear-representation]. Thus they define tangent vectors $Y_s,Y_n$. Comparing coefficients using [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus] gives $dr_V(Y_s)=S_V$ and $dr_V(Y_n)=N_V$ for every $V$.

source.place: Agent solution of exercise 17.74 using Theorem 9.2, pp.164--165, with R the dual numbers; 10.6--10.7.

proof.text: The linearity and bracket preservation of [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus] give $di(Y_s+Y_n)=S_i+N_i=di(Y)$ and $di([Y_s,Y_n])=S_iN_i-N_iS_i=0$. Injectivity from step 1 gives $Y=Y_s+Y_n$ and $[Y_s,Y_n]=0$. Step 3 already gives the required representation identities. Any other pair satisfying the statement has, in representation $i$, the same unique matrix parts by [lem-sfb-additive-jordan-linear-compatibility]; injectivity gives equality of the two pairs. This also proves uniqueness if only commuting semisimple and nilpotent images in every representation were specified.

source.place: Agent solution of Proposition 17.74(a), p.377: matrix equality and faithfulness.

proof.text: Let $f:H\to H'$ be a homomorphism over perfect $k$. For every rational representation $r'$ of $H'$, apply step 3 to $r'\circ f$. The chain rule [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus] gives $dr'(df(Y_s))=(dr'(df(Y)))_s$ and the corresponding nilpotent identity. Apply the same construction to $df(Y)$ in $H'$. Choose a faithful closed representation of $H'$ by [lem-sfb-affine-group-faithful-linear-representation]; its injective differential shows $df(Y_s)=(df(Y))_s$ and $df(Y_n)=(df(Y))_n$.

source.place: Proposition 17.74(b), p.377; argument through composite rational representations.

proof.text: Let $K/k$ be an extension of perfect fields. Identify $\operatorname{Lie}(H_K)$ with $K\otimes_k\mathfrak h$ using [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus]. By [lem-sfb-additive-jordan-linear-compatibility], the parts of $di_K(1\otimes Y)=1\otimes di(Y)$ are $1\otimes di(Y_s)$ and $1\otimes di(Y_n)$. Construct the parts of $1\otimes Y$ over $K$ by steps 2--4. Their images under $di_K$ are those same matrix parts. Injectivity from step 1 gives $(1\otimes Y)_s=1\otimes Y_s$ and $(1\otimes Y)_n=1\otimes Y_n$. Representations over $K$ need not descend to $k$.

source.place: Preliminaries on p.376 and Theorem 9.11 scalar-extension uniqueness, pp.168--169; 10.19, p.192.

proof.text: Now take arbitrary $k$ and the given closed immersion $i$ of the statement. It is injective on algebra-valued points: on affine coordinate rings it is a surjection, and two maps out of the quotient agreeing after that surjection are equal [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Thus $di$ and $di_{\bar k}$ are injective by the dual-number argument of step 1 [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus]. The algebraic closure $\bar k$ is perfect: its irreducible polynomials are linear, hence separable. Apply steps 2--4 to $Y_{\bar k}$. If $di(Y)$ is geometrically semisimple, its extended matrix has parts $di_{\bar k}(Y_{\bar k})$ and zero; if it is nilpotent, its extended matrix has parts zero and $di_{\bar k}(Y_{\bar k})$. These identifications follow from uniqueness in [lem-sfb-additive-jordan-linear-compatibility]. Injectivity forces respectively $(Y_{\bar k})_n=0$ or $(Y_{\bar k})_s=0$.

source.place: Proposition 17.74 over the algebraic closure; 10.14, p.190. Geometric formulation supplied explicitly.

proof.text: For any given rational $r$ over $k$, extend it to $\bar k$. By step 3, $dr_{\bar k}(Y_{\bar k})$ has parts $dr_{\bar k}((Y_{\bar k})_s)$ and $dr_{\bar k}((Y_{\bar k})_n)$, using the scalar-extension differential identification [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus]. In the first case of step 7 the nilpotent part is zero, so this matrix is diagonalizable; this is exactly geometric semisimplicity of $dr(Y)$. In the second case its semisimple part is zero, so a positive power of it is zero. That power is obtained by entrywise extension of $(dr(Y))^q$; injectivity of $k\to\bar k$ makes each entry of $(dr(Y))^q$ zero. Thus $dr(Y)$ is nilpotent. All representations used are algebraic group representations, as required.

source.place: Geometric faithful detection deduced from Proposition 17.74(a), p.377; scalar extension as in 10.19.

proof_origin.place: Exercise Proposition 17.74, p.377, solved using Theorem 9.2 over dual numbers and additive linear Jordan compatibility; Sections 10.6--10.23 supply tangent functoriality. Milne states this proposition without a proof.
